newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ruling party seeks election landslide. [CORRECTED 10:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Singapore ruling party seeks election landslide. [CORRECTED 10:30 GMT]

text.p: Singaporeans voted in a general election on Thursday with Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's ruling party already assured of victory but fighting to maintain its near-complete dominance of parliament.
Goh's People's Action Party already sealed a majority in the 83-member parliament because the opposition contested only 36 seats.

But Goh, whose party faced no opposition in the city-state's parliament for 13 years until 1981 (corrects to delete reference to independence) sees losing even one seat as an effective defeat and has staked his prestige on limiting opposition representation.
Opposition parties won just four of the 81 parliamentary seats in the last general election in 1991. The next parliament will be enlarged by two seats through boundary changes.
Goh, returned unopposed in his own seat, visited a key constituency, Cheng San, on Thursday to drum up support.
Cheng San, a multi-member constituency which elects five MPs in a winner-takes-all contest, has seen a strong challenge from the opposition Workers' Party (WP).
Political analysts said defeat for the PAP in Cheng San, which might double the opposition's seats, could damage Goh's reputation as a strong leader capable of winning elections.
"If the opposition wins eight to 10 seats, it could jeopardise Goh's premiership," said Bruce Gale, an analyst at Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.
Goh and deputy prime ministers Lee Hsien Loong and Tony Tan entered the fray in Cheng San this week, saying the vote there would be a test of their leadership.
Lee told reporters that victory for the PAP in the constituency was vital: "A lot is at stake," he said.
The PAP has ruled Singapore since 1959, transforming it through strict control into a prosperous city where average per capita income is higher than in Britain, the old colonial power.
But opposition parties say they want alternative voices in parliament and a check on the PAP's dominance.
Goh said on Thursday he was confident of victory in Cheng San and that he had staked his reputation on winning there.

Goh has called one WP candidate in Cheng San, Tang Liang Hong, a "Chinese chauvinist", saying Tan's views pose a threat to Singapore's multi-racial society, which is 77 percent Chinese but has significant minorities of Malays and Indians.

Goh and leading ministers have repeatedly threatened that areas which return opposition candidates would miss out on a multi-billion dollar programme to upgrade public housing. Goh has said these areas would become slums in 20 to 30 years' time.
On Thursday, Goh rejected complaints that the threats were unfair.
"In a war, when you have to ration food, you give to your own soldiers first," he told reporters.

Alleged U.S. meddling also became a factor in campaigning after the Foreign Ministry last week described as "interference in Singapore's domestic politics" a comment by a U.S. official criticising linking votes with housing funds.

A 60-year old Singapore man leaving a polling station on Thursday said he disapproved of the PAP's threats but would still vote for the party. "For all my grouses, I cannot cut off my nose to spite my face. I will vote for the PAP."
But another voter decried "the government's high-handedness" and said he had voted for the opposition.
Polls close at 8 p.m. (1200 GMT). Results are not expected until after midnight (1600 GMT). About 765,000 voters were due to vote in the contested seats. Voting is compulsory.
